docs.title: AOD4184 (D4184) MOSFET Module — AC001
docs.text: Aliases: D4184 / AOD4184 “MOSFET relay” module (various vendors) Category: AC

docs.title: Quick Facts
docs.text:
• Type: N-channel MOSFET low-side switch (module). You put the load between LOAD and +, the module switches the ground side.
  • Logic: Accepts MCU input (3.3–5 V on most modules)
  • Current: Marketing says “50 A”, but real-world continuous is ~10 A @ 12 V without extra heatsinking due to PCB thermal limits.

docs.title: Links
docs.text: • Where to buy: AliExpress

docs.title: Typical Pinout (varies by seller)
docs.text:
• Power side: + (to supply +), LOAD (to load’s negative end), - must be connected to supply - and GND of esp
  • Control side: PWM: Connect to GPIO, GND: Connect to GND from esp.

docs.title: Wiring (ESP32 → 12 V fan example)
docs.text:
• 12 V + → + on module, 12 V − → module GND (power ground).
  • Fan + → 12 V +; fan − → LOAD on module.
  • ESP32 GPIO (e.g., GPIO 23) → PWM on module; ESP32 GND → module GND.

Remember: Load goes between LOAD and +. The module sinks current to ground (low-side).

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text: • Audible ringing with PWM: Buzz often comes from the load/PSU when you PWM in the audible band (<20 kHz). Two easy fixes: use time-proportioning (slow duty cycling) with multi-second periods (see example below) or push PWM >20 kHz.

docs.title: Code — Easiest: 5s ON, 5s OFF (ESP32 / Arduino)
docs.text:
// AC001: D4184 / AOD4184 module test — 5s ON, 5s OFF
// Wire: ESP32 GPIO 23 -> IN, GNDs common
const int RELAY_PIN = 23;

void setup() {
  pinMode(RELAY_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW); // start OFF
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, HIGH); // ON
  delay(5000);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);  // OFF
  delay(5000);
}

docs.title: Code - "x% power" without audible whine (slow time-proportioning)
docs.text:
// AC001: Time-proportioning control (TPC) with a long period (no audible PWM)
const int RELAY_PIN = 23;

// set desired power level (0–100)
int power_percent = 30;           // e.g., 30% average power
const unsigned long PERIOD_MS = 10000; // 10s cycle

void setup() {
  pinMode(RELAY_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);
}

void loop() {
  unsigned long on_ms  = (PERIOD_MS * power_percent) / 100;
  unsigned long off_ms = PERIOD_MS - on_ms;

  if (on_ms > 0) {
    digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, HIGH);
    delay(on_ms);
  }
  if (off_ms > 0) {
    digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, LOW);
    delay(off_ms);
  }
}

docs.title: 99-S12 smart cabinet electromagnetic lock - AC005
docs.text: Compact 12 V fail‑secure solenoid bolt used for cabinets, drawers and small doors. When powered, the bolt retracts (unlock). When unpowered, the spring pushes the bolt out (lock). Ideal when you need a simple latch you can pulse from an ESP32 via a MOSFET or relay—no position sensing built‑in.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Datasheet: Similar model (Multicomp Pro MP001163) PDF — dimensions & duty‑cycle are indicative, exact values may differ from 99‑S12.
  • Tutorial: ESP32 controlling a solenoid lock (wiring + code): ESP32IO

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Extracted from vendor listings for 99‑S12 (values vary by batch/variant):

  • Operating voltage: 12 V DC ("12 V universal")
  • Current: variants listed around 0.35 A / 0.6 A / 1.2 A (instantaneous trigger) — measure your unit
  • Pull stroke (throw): 0–4 mm
  • Pull force: at 4 mm ≥ 80 g (typ. at 0.35 A)
  • Retention: at 0 mm ≥ 120 g
  • Operating mode: power‑on = unlock; power‑off = lock (fail‑secure)
  • Duty / interval note: listing states “power on 90%, interval” — treat as intermittent duty (use short pulses)
  • Ambient: −25 °C to +80 °C; RH 45–80 %
  • Withstand voltage: AC 1000 V; Insulation resistance: 50 MΩ
  • Leads: 2‑wire pigtail
  • Life: up to 1,000,000 cycles (vendor‑stated)

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text: This part is just the actuator, no PCB: - Red (+12 V) — connect to +12 V supply. - Black (GND) — connect to MOSFET/relay side to switch return to ground. (No logic pins, no addresses.)

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
ESP32 cannot drive the lock directly. Use a logic‑level N‑MOSFET or a relay module.

MOSFET option (recommended for speed/size): - 12 V + → lock red wire. - Lock black wire → DRAIN of N‑MOSFET (e.g., IRLZ44N, AOZ/AOD logic‑level types). - SOURCE → 0 V (GND). - GATE → ESP32 GPIO via ~100 Ω; add 10 kΩ gate pull‑down to GND. - Flyback diode across the lock (e.g., 1N5819/1N4007): anode to MOSFET side, cathode to +12 V. - Common ground: tie ESP32 GND to 12 V supply GND.

Relay option: ESP32 → Relay IN; relay switches 12 V to the lock. Still add a flyback diode across the coil if your relay board doesn’t have one.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Treat as intermittent duty: use short pulses (e.g., 100–500 ms) to unlock; avoid long holds or it will heat up.
  • Current varies by batch (0.35 A–1.2 A). Bench‑measure your unit and size wiring/MOSFET accordingly.
  • Always use a flyback diode; without it you risk brown‑outs or ESP32 resets.
  • Fail‑secure behavior: loses power ⇒ locks. Plan for power‑loss scenarios.

docs.title: How to use (ESP32 / Arduino)
docs.text:
Simple pulse‑to‑unlock using a MOSFET (active‑HIGH gate). No external libraries needed.

// GPIO driving a logic-level N-MOSFET gate through ~100Ω
const int LOCK_PIN = 16;  // choose any suitable GPIO

void setup() {
  pinMode(LOCK_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(LOCK_PIN, LOW); // ensure locked (no power to solenoid)
}

// Pulse to unlock for 200 ms
void unlockPulse(uint16_t ms = 200) {
  digitalWrite(LOCK_PIN, HIGH);  // power the solenoid => unlock
  delay(ms);
  digitalWrite(LOCK_PIN, LOW);   // remove power => lock
}

void loop() {
  // Example: unlock for 200 ms every 5 seconds
  unlockPulse(200);
  delay(5000);
}

If you use a relay module instead of a MOSFET, replace LOCK_PIN wiring accordingly (some boards are active‑LOW).

docs.title: WS2812B - AC006
docs.text: Individually addressable RGB LED in a 5050 SMD package with an integrated controller (“NeoPixel”‑compatible). Uses a single‑wire 800 kbps protocol to daisy‑chain many LEDs with 24‑bit color (GRB). Runs from ~5 V and is ideal for status lights, indicators, light bars and small animations.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Datasheet: PDF
  • Tutorial: Random Nerd Tutorials

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• Package: 5050 SMD, 1 LED + integrated driver per pixel.
  • Supply: Typically 5 V (electrical characteristics given for VDD=4.5–5.5 V). Absolute supply rating listed as +3.5 to +5.3 V.
  • Logic levels: DIN VIH ≥ 0.7×VDD (so at 5 V, ≥3.5 V), VIL ≤ 0.3×VDD.
  • Data rate: 800 kbps single‑wire; GRB byte order.
  • PWM scan freq: ≥ 400 Hz.
  • Chaining: signal reshaping each pixel; at 30 fps, “not less than” ~1024 pixels.
  • Timing (±150 ns): T0H≈0.4 µs, T0L≈0.85 µs, T1H≈0.8 µs, T1L≈0.45 µs; reset low ≥ 50 µs.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
• VDD — +5 V supply
  • DIN — Data in (from MCU / previous LED)
  • VSS — Ground
  • DOUT — Data out (to next LED)

Pin names and order per datasheet. Decouple each LED with a local 0.1 µF capacitor (shown as “104” in the typical circuit).

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
ESP32 → WS2812B (single LED or strip):

  • Power the LEDs from a stable 5 V rail. Tie GND (ESP32) to VSS (LED).
  • Drive DIN from an ESP32 GPIO through a ~330–470 Ω series resistor.
  • Place a large electrolytic (e.g., 470–1000 µF) across the 5 V rail near first LED to absorb inrush.
  • Level shifting: Because VIH is 0.7×VDD, a 3.3 V ESP32 output is below spec when LEDs run at 5 V. Use a proper level shifter (e.g., SN74AHCT125/74HCT14) or run the LEDs closer to 4.5 V so 3.3 V meets VIH, if your setup allows.
  • For long runs, inject 5 V power every 1–2 m and at both ends. Keep data wire short and alongside ground.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Don’t drive DIN when LEDs are unpowered (add series resistor + ensure common GND).
  • 3.3 V logic into 5 V‑powered LEDs is out‑of‑spec per VIH; many strips work but it’s not guaranteed—prefer level shifting.
  • Start‑up can draw a surge; oversize the 5 V supply and add bulk capacitance.
  • GRB color order (not RGB) is expected by default.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
Arduino (ESP32) with Adafruit_NeoPixel

#include <Adafruit_NeoPixel.h>
#define LED_PIN  5          // pick any PWM-capable GPIO
#define LED_CNT  8          // number of pixels
Adafruit_NeoPixel strip(LED_CNT, LED_PIN, NEO_GRB + NEO_KHZ800);

void setup() {
  strip.begin();
  strip.show();             // turn off all pixels
  strip.setBrightness(64);  // 0..255
}

void loop() {
  // simple color wipe
  for (int i = 0; i < LED_CNT; i++) {
    strip.setPixelColor(i, strip.Color(255, 0, 0)); // red
    strip.show();
    delay(50);
  }
}

Libraries: Adafruit NeoPixel or FastLED (PlatformIO/Arduino Library Manager).

docs.title: Ultrasonic Nebulizer Driver - AC007
docs.text: A small driver board for ultrasonic atomizer discs (≈20 mm piezo, ~108–113 kHz). These boards create a cool visible mist by pushing water through a porous mesh at ultrasonic frequency. Use when you need quick humidification or fog effects in enclosures, incubators, props, or scent projects. These particular boards are power‑only devices (no documented control I/O); you typically switch their 5 V power from a microcontroller.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy (6‑nozzle): AliExpress
  • Where to buy (dual‑nozzle): AliExpress
  • Datasheet (transducer specs): STEMinc 20 mm / 113 kHz atomizer
  • Tutorials / build ideas:
    • Seeed Studio “Grove – Water Atomization”
    • CircuitDigest “Ultrasonic Mist Maker using ESP‑01”

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Six‑nozzle board (from listing):

  • Supply: 5 V (USB‑C)
  • Current / Power: ~300 mA board rating; recommend ≥ 2 A 5 V supply (seller notes “Minimum 2A”)
  • Power: 2.5–3 W
  • Atomization frequency: 108 kHz ± 2 kHz
  • Modes: six‑spray / dynamic / single / multiple (mode cycling on board)
  • PCB: FR‑4, 1.2 mm
  • Module size: 65 × 30 mm; disc connector: PH2.0 to 20 mm atomizer tablets (aperture 4–5 µm)
  • Accessories: brackets + cotton wicks (per kit)

Dual‑nozzle board (from listing):

  • Power: 2–3 W, intended for USB 5 V sources
  • Operating temperature (claimed): −40 … +80 °C
  • Other details are vague in seller text; treat as a similar 5 V 108–113 kHz atomizer driver. If critical, verify with the exact board in hand.

Atomizer discs (typical 20 mm metal‑mesh):

  • Resonant frequency: ~113 kHz
  • Droplet size: ≈10 µm
  • Rated input at the disc: tens of Vp‑p driven by the board (do not drive discs directly from GPIO)
  • Example transducer specs: see “Datasheet” link above.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
These boards are usually power‑only:

  • USB‑C 5 V in (or VBUS/GND pads if provided)
  • Disc connectors (JST‑PH 2.0) to the piezo atomizer tablets

Some variants expose a push‑button to change spray modes. No documented logic‑level control pins are provided on the referenced listings.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Goal: switch the board’s 5 V power from an ESP32.

  • Provide a separate 5 V supply rated ≥ 2 A for multi‑nozzle boards. Do not power from the ESP32 or USB hub ports.
  • Switch power using one of:
  • A 5 V relay module (easy, but bulky/noisy), or
  • A high‑side P‑MOSFET load switch board rated ≥ 2–3 A (preferred for silence/efficiency).
  • Common ground between ESP32 and the 5 V supply/load switch. Keep high‑current 5 V traces short and away from the ESP32 RF.
  • Keep the atomizer away from electronics; condensation is real. Use a splash guard and route the mist upward.

Minimal wiring (P‑MOSFET switch):

  • ESP32 GPIO → gate driver/control of the load‑switch module
  • Load‑switch VIN = 5 V, VOUT → humidifier board VBUS
  • Grounds tied together

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• These boards do not accept ESP32 GPIO control directly; you must switch their 5 V.
  • Current spikes at start‑up can reset your system—use a stout 5 V supply and short wiring.
  • Moisture will corrode boards: mount vertically, add drip protection, and avoid enclosed spaces without airflow.
  • Atomizer discs are consumables; performance drops over time. Keep spare 20 mm, ~108–113 kHz discs.
  • If your board cycles “modes,” that behavior is internal; it can’t be set digitally unless your specific PCB exposes pads (not documented here).

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
Example: toggle the mist with a GPIO driving a typical active‑low EN pin on a P‑channel high‑side load‑switch module. Uses only Arduino.h on an ESP32.

// ESP32: toggle a 5V load switch controlling the nebulizer board
const int MIST_EN = 15;   // connect to load-switch EN (active-low or -high varies by board)
bool activeLow = true;    // set according to your switch board

void setup() {
  pinMode(MIST_EN, OUTPUT);
  // default off
  digitalWrite(MIST_EN, activeLow ? HIGH : LOW);
}

void mistOn()  { digitalWrite(MIST_EN, activeLow ? LOW : HIGH); }
void mistOff() { digitalWrite(MIST_EN, activeLow ? HIGH : LOW); }

void loop() {
  mistOn();
  delay(10 * 1000);   // 10 s ON
  mistOff();
  delay(20 * 1000);   // 20 s OFF
}

Libraries: none (plain Arduino core). If using a relay module, drive its IN pin instead. For humidity‑based control, pair with a SHT4x/DHT22 and implement simple on/off hysteresis.

docs.title: 1-Channel Relay Module - AC008
docs.text: Single-channel relay board with optocoupler input and jumper-selectable trigger level (HIGH or LOW). Use it to safely switch mains or higher-current DC loads from an ESP32 GPIO via an isolated input stage. Typical variants are available with 5 V or 12 V coils. If you need more than one channel, use multi‑relay boards instead.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Tutorial: Random Nerd Tutorials – ESP32 Relay Module (Web Server)

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• Optocoupler‑isolated input stage
  • Operating voltage (coil): 5 V or 12 V (board variant)
  • Trigger: HIGH or LOW selectable via on‑board jumper
  • Indicators: Power LED and Relay status LED
  • Max load: AC 250 V / 10 A, DC 30 V / 10 A (depends on relay fitted; verify on your part)
  • Control input IN requires ≳ 4 mA drive current (from listing)
  • Output contacts: COM, NO, (NC is present on most modules even if the listing only calls out COM)

Values above were taken from the AliExpress listing. If your board has a different relay model, follow that relay's datasheet limits.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
Header / screw terminals (I/O side): - DC+ (VCC): Board power for the input/driver (5 V or 12 V version) - DC− (GND): Ground - IN: Control input from microcontroller - Jumper: Selects HIGH or LOW trigger

Relay terminals (load side): - COM: Common contact - NO: Normally‑Open (closes to COM when active) - NC: Normally‑Closed (opens from COM when active)

Some one‑channel boards expose COM/NO only; others provide COM/NO/NC.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Assuming a 5 V relay module with an ESP32:

  • Power the module DC+ = 5 V, DC− = GND from a 5 V supply. (Don’t power the relay coil from the ESP32 3.3 V pin.)
  • Connect ESP32 GND ↔ DC− (common ground).
  • Connect an ESP32 GPIO (e.g., GPIO 26) to IN.
  • Place the jumper to match your preferred trigger (LOW or HIGH).
  • Wire your load to the COM/NO/NC screw terminals as needed. For mains, break only one conductor (active/hot) and keep neutral/earth intact.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Mains safety: Treat anything on the relay terminals as high voltage. Use proper creepage/clearance and insulated enclosures. If unsure, stick to low‑voltage DC loads.
  • Active‑LOW vs ACTIVE‑HIGH: Many boards default to active‑LOW. Use the jumper to choose, and match it in code.
  • Board variants: Some modules have separate JD‑VCC/VCC pins for true opto‑isolation; this board appears to use DC+/DC− only (shared ground).
  • Contact ratings: 10 A is the maximum under ideal conditions. For inductive loads (motors, solenoids), derate and consider snubbers/RC or MOVs.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
Very simple example (Arduino framework on ESP32). Adjust RELAY_ACTIVE to LOW or HIGH to match your jumper setting, and pick a free GPIO.

// 1-Channel Relay Module (optocoupler) – ESP32 example
// Requires no special libraries

const int RELAY_PIN = 26;          // choose any suitable GPIO
const int RELAY_ACTIVE = LOW;      // set to LOW or HIGH to match jumper
const int RELAY_INACTIVE = (RELAY_ACTIVE == LOW) ? HIGH : LOW;

void setup() {
  pinMode(RELAY_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, RELAY_INACTIVE);
}

void loop() {
  // Toggle the relay every 2 seconds
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, RELAY_ACTIVE);
  delay(2000);
  digitalWrite(RELAY_PIN, RELAY_INACTIVE);
  delay(2000);
}

docs.title: Standard 5mm LEDs - AC011
docs.text: Assorted 5mm through-hole LEDs for indicator lights, status displays, and visual feedback. Includes single-color LEDs (red, blue, green, yellow, white) and RGB LEDs. Standard forward voltage ~2-3.5V depending on color. Use with current-limiting resistors (typically 220Ω-1kΩ for 3.3V/5V systems).

docs.title: Available Colors
docs.text:
Single-color LEDs:

  • Red: ~2.0V forward voltage, 20mA typical
  • Green: ~2.1V forward voltage, 20mA typical
  • Blue: ~3.2V forward voltage, 20mA typical
  • Yellow: ~2.1V forward voltage, 20mA typical
  • White: ~3.2V forward voltage, 20mA typical

RGB LEDs:

  • Common cathode or common anode
  • 4 pins: R, G, B, Common
  • Each color channel: 20mA max

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress - 5mm LED Assortment
  • Tutorial: ESP32 LED Control (Random Nerd)

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• Package: 5mm (F5) through-hole
  • Lens: Clear or diffused (varies by color)
  • Forward current: 20mA typical, 30mA max
  • Viewing angle: ~20-30° (clear), ~60° (diffused)
  • Lifespan: ~50,000 hours typical

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Single LED with current-limiting resistor:

ESP32 GPIO → Resistor (220Ω-1kΩ) → LED Anode (+) → LED Cathode (-) → GND

Resistor calculation:

  • For 3.3V GPIO: R = (3.3V - Vf) / 0.02A
  • Example (red LED, Vf=2.0V): R = (3.3 - 2.0) / 0.02 = 65Ω → use 220Ω for safety
  • Example (blue LED, Vf=3.2V): R = (3.3 - 3.2) / 0.02 = 5Ω → use 100Ω minimum

RGB LED (common cathode): 

GPIO_R → Resistor → R pin
GPIO_G → Resistor → G pin
GPIO_B → Resistor → B pin
Common → GND

docs.title: Identifying LED Pins
docs.text:
• Flat edge: Indicates cathode (-) side
  • Longer leg: Anode (+)
  • Shorter leg: Cathode (-)
  • RGB: Longest pin is usually the common pin

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Always use current-limiting resistors - connecting directly to GPIO will damage the LED and/or ESP32
  • Blue/white LEDs need higher voltage (~3.2V) - may be dim on 3.3V systems
  • Check polarity - LEDs only work in one direction
  • RGB common anode vs cathode - verify your LED type before wiring
  • PWM for dimming - use LEDC on ESP32 for brightness control

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
Simple blink (ESP32):

const int LED_PIN = 2;  // any GPIO

void setup() {
  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
}

void loop() {
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
  delay(1000);
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
  delay(1000);
}

PWM brightness control:

const int LED_PIN = 2;
const int PWM_CHANNEL = 0;

void setup() {
  ledcSetup(PWM_CHANNEL, 5000, 8);  // 5kHz, 8-bit
  ledcAttachPin(LED_PIN, PWM_CHANNEL);
}

void loop() {
  // Fade in
  for (int brightness = 0; brightness <= 255; brightness++) {
    ledcWrite(PWM_CHANNEL, brightness);
    delay(5);
  }
  // Fade out
  for (int brightness = 255; brightness >= 0; brightness--) {
    ledcWrite(PWM_CHANNEL, brightness);
    delay(5);
  }
}

RGB LED control (common cathode):

const int PIN_R = 25;
const int PIN_G = 26;
const int PIN_B = 27;

void setup() {
  ledcSetup(0, 5000, 8);
  ledcSetup(1, 5000, 8);
  ledcSetup(2, 5000, 8);
  ledcAttachPin(PIN_R, 0);
  ledcAttachPin(PIN_G, 1);
  ledcAttachPin(PIN_B, 2);
}

void setColor(int r, int g, int b) {
  ledcWrite(0, r);
  ledcWrite(1, g);
  ledcWrite(2, b);
}

void loop() {
  setColor(255, 0, 0);    // Red
  delay(1000);
  setColor(0, 255, 0);    // Green
  delay(1000);
  setColor(0, 0, 255);    // Blue
  delay(1000);
  setColor(255, 255, 0);  // Yellow
  delay(1000);
}

docs.title: 12V DC Solenoid Valve 1/2" (Normally Closed) - AC012
docs.text: Electrically-controlled water valve with 1/2" (DN15) threaded connections. Normally closed design - opens when 12V DC is applied, closes when power is removed.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Voltage 12V DC Current ~300-500mA (coil) Power ~5-6W Connection size 1/2" NPT or G1/2" (check marking) Port type 2-way, normally closed (NC) Pressure rating 0-0.8 MPa (0-116 PSI) Flow direction Marked with arrow on body Media Water, air, non-corrosive liquids Temperature 0-80°C (liquid temp) Body material Brass or plastic (check specs) Seal material NBR (nitrile rubber) Quantity 4 pieces

docs.title: Pinout / Connections
docs.text:
Electrical (coil):

  • 2 wire leads (red/black or unmarked)
  • Polarity: Not sensitive (DC coil, either direction works)

Plumbing:

  • Inlet: Marked with arrow (flow direction)
  • Outlet: Opposite side
  • Threading: 1/2" male NPT or G1/2" threads

docs.title: Operation
docs.text:
Normally Closed (NC):

  • Power OFF → Valve closed (no flow)
  • Power ON (12V DC) → Valve opens (allows flow)
  • Spring returns valve to closed position when power removed

docs.title: Typical Wiring (with MOSFET)
docs.text:
+12V
  |
  +--- Solenoid Coil ---|>|--- +
                               |
                          Drain (D)
                        IRLZ44N (AC301)
ESP32 GPIO ---[220Ω]--- Gate (G)

10kΓ                   Source (S)
  |                         |
GND ----------------------GND

Diode: 1N4007 or 1N5819 (flyback protection - REQUIRED!)

Never connect solenoid directly to GPIO - use relay (AC008) or MOSFET (AC301).

docs.title: Example Code (ESP32 + MOSFET)
docs.text:
// Solenoid control via MOSFET
#define VALVE_PIN 25

void setup() {
  pinMode(VALVE_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(VALVE_PIN, LOW);  // Valve closed initially
}

void valve_open() {
  digitalWrite(VALVE_PIN, HIGH);  // Apply 12V
}

void valve_close() {
  digitalWrite(VALVE_PIN, LOW);   // Remove power
}

// Timed watering example
void water_for(unsigned long milliseconds) {
  valve_open();
  delay(milliseconds);
  valve_close();
}

docs.title: Plumbing Installation
docs.text:
Threading:

  1. Wrap threads with PTFE tape (Teflon tape) - 3-5 wraps clockwise
  2. Hand-tighten into fitting
  3. Use wrench for final 1-2 turns (don't overtighten)

Flow direction: Arrow on valve body shows correct flow direction (inlet → outlet).

Pressure: Requires minimum pressure (0.02-0.05 MPa) to seal properly. Won't work well with gravity-fed systems at very low pressure.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
1. Flyback diode required: MUST use 1N4007 or similar across coil to protect MOSFET/relay
  2. Inrush current: Initial energizing can spike to 1A briefly
  3. Minimum pressure: Needs some water pressure to seal - may leak at very low pressure
  4. Flow direction: Install with arrow pointing from inlet to outlet
  5. Power consumption: Coil draws 300-500mA continuously when open (not suitable for battery operation)
  6. Thread type: Check if NPT or G-thread (may need adapter)
  7. Water hammer: Closing valve quickly can cause pressure spike in pipes

docs.title: Power Options
docs.text:
12V power supply:

  • Wall adapter (1A or higher)
  • Car battery
  • 3S LiPo battery (11.1-12.6V)
  • Lead-acid battery

NOT suitable for:

  • 5V USB power (voltage too low)
  • Small batteries (current draw too high)

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
Automated irrigation: Timed or sensor-based garden watering

Aquarium/pond: Water change automation, top-off systems

Hydroponics: Nutrient solution control

Washing systems: Car wash, pet wash automation

Safety shutoff: Emergency water shutoff valve

docs.title: Example Project: Smart Irrigation
docs.text:
// Soil moisture sensor + solenoid valve
#define MOISTURE_PIN 34   // Analog input
#define VALVE_PIN    25   // Solenoid control

void loop() {
  int moisture = analogRead(MOISTURE_PIN);

  // If soil is dry (reading < 1000), water for 10 seconds
  if (moisture < 1000) {
    digitalWrite(VALVE_PIN, HIGH);  // Open valve
    delay(10000);                   // Water for 10s
    digitalWrite(VALVE_PIN, LOW);   // Close valve
    delay(3600000);                 // Wait 1 hour before checking again
  }

  delay(60000);  // Check every minute
}

docs.title: Water Pressure Sensor (G1/4 Thread, 0-1.2MPa) - AC013
docs.text: Analog voltage output pressure transducer for monitoring water pressure in pipes and systems. G1/4" threaded connection, 0.5-4.5V output proportional to pressure.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Pressure range 0 - 1.2 MPa (0-174 PSI, 0-12 bar) Output type Analog voltage (0.5V - 4.5V) Supply voltage 5V DC Output range 0.5V @ 0 MPa, 4.5V @ 1.2 MPa Accuracy ±1.5% FS (full scale) Thread size G1/4" male Response time <2ms Media Water, air, non-corrosive liquids/gases Temperature -20°C to 85°C (compensated 0-50°C) Protection IP65 (with connector sealed) Cable length ~1m (3-wire: +5V, GND, Signal)

docs.title: Pinout / Wiring
docs.text:
3 wires (typically):

  • Red: +5V (power supply)
  • Black: GND (ground)
  • Yellow/White/Green: Signal (0.5-4.5V output)

Output voltage formula:

V_out = 0.5V + (Pressure_MPa / 1.2) × 4.0V

Examples:

  • 0 MPa → 0.5V
  • 0.6 MPa → 2.5V
  • 1.2 MPa → 4.5V

docs.title: Typical Wiring (ESP32)
docs.text:
Sensor Red    → ESP32 5V (or external 5V supply)
Sensor Black  → ESP32 GND
Sensor Signal → ESP32 GPIO34 (ADC pin)

Note: ESP32 ADC max is 3.3V, so pressures above ~0.7 MPa will saturate the ADC. Use voltage divider or external ADC for full range.

docs.title: Example Code (ESP32)
docs.text:
// Pressure sensor on ADC pin
#define PRESSURE_PIN 34

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  analogSetAttenuation(ADC_11db);  // 0-3.3V range
}

void loop() {
  int adc_value = analogRead(PRESSURE_PIN);

  // Convert ADC to voltage (12-bit ADC, 0-4095)
  float voltage = (adc_value / 4095.0) * 3.3;

  // Convert voltage to pressure (MPa)
  // V_out = 0.5 + (P / 1.2) * 4.0
  // P = ((V_out - 0.5) / 4.0) * 1.2
  float pressure_mpa = ((voltage - 0.5) / 4.0) * 1.2;

  // Clamp to valid range
  if (pressure_mpa < 0) pressure_mpa = 0;
  if (pressure_mpa > 1.2) pressure_mpa = 1.2;

  // Convert to other units
  float pressure_bar = pressure_mpa * 10.0;
  float pressure_psi = pressure_mpa * 145.038;

  Serial.print("ADC: ");
  Serial.print(adc_value);
  Serial.print(" | Voltage: ");
  Serial.print(voltage, 2);
  Serial.print("V | Pressure: ");
  Serial.print(pressure_mpa, 2);
  Serial.print(" MPa (");
  Serial.print(pressure_bar, 1);
  Serial.print(" bar, ");
  Serial.print(pressure_psi, 1);
  Serial.println(" PSI)");

  delay(1000);
}

docs.title: Voltage Divider for Full Range
docs.text:
If you need to measure full 0-1.2 MPa range (0.5-4.5V output) with ESP32 (3.3V ADC):

Sensor Signal ---[10kΩ]---+---[22kΩ]--- GND
                           |
                      ESP32 ADC Pin

Divider ratio: 22k / (10k + 22k) = 0.688

  • 4.5V input → 3.1V at ADC (safe)
  • 0.5V input → 0.34V at ADC

Adjust formula accordingly:

float voltage_sensor = voltage_adc / 0.688;
float pressure_mpa = ((voltage_sensor - 0.5) / 4.0) * 1.2;

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Plumbing:

  1. Wrap G1/4" threads with PTFE tape (3-5 wraps)
  2. Thread into G1/4" female port or adapter
  3. Hand-tighten, then wrench for final turn (don't overtighten)
  4. Ensure flow direction doesn't matter (sensor measures static pressure)

Electrical:

  1. Connect wires to microcontroller ADC pin
  2. Use twisted-pair or shielded cable if running long distances
  3. Seal cable entry point if outdoor/wet installation

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
1. ESP32 ADC limit: 3.3V max - use voltage divider or external ADC for full range
  2. Offset voltage: 0.5V offset (not 0V) at zero pressure
  3. Power supply: Needs stable 5V - use good regulator, not USB directly
  4. Thread sealant: Use PTFE tape, not liquid sealant (can clog sensor port)
  5. Pressure spikes: Water hammer can briefly exceed max pressure - add snubber if needed
  6. Accuracy: ±1.5% error means ±0.018 MPa (±2.6 PSI) uncertainty
  7. Media compatibility: Water/air only - don't use with oils or corrosive liquids

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
For best accuracy, calibrate with known pressure:

  1. Zero point: Disconnect from pressure source (atmospheric pressure) - should read ~0.5V
  2. Full scale: Apply known pressure (e.g., 0.6 MPa / 87 PSI) - verify output voltage
  3. Adjust formula: Correct offset and scale factor in code

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
Water system monitoring: Home/garden water pressure

Pump control: Turn pump on/off based on pressure

Leak detection: Detect pressure drop indicating leak

Irrigation automation: Coordinate with solenoid valve (AC012)

Aquarium/pond: Monitor filter pump pressure

docs.title: Example Project: Pump Auto-Shutoff
docs.text:
#define PRESSURE_PIN 34
#define PUMP_PIN     25

float pressure_threshold_low  = 0.3;  // MPa (turn pump ON)
float pressure_threshold_high = 0.8;  // MPa (turn pump OFF)

void loop() {
  float voltage = (analogRead(PRESSURE_PIN) / 4095.0) * 3.3;
  float pressure_mpa = ((voltage - 0.5) / 4.0) * 1.2;

  if (pressure_mpa < pressure_threshold_low) {
    digitalWrite(PUMP_PIN, HIGH);  // Start pump
  } else if (pressure_mpa > pressure_threshold_high) {
    digitalWrite(PUMP_PIN, LOW);   // Stop pump
  }

  delay(1000);
}

docs.text:

docs.title: IRLZ44N N-Channel Power MOSFET (Logic-Level, TO-220) - AC301
docs.text: Logic-level N-channel power MOSFET in TO-220 package. Perfect for switching high-current loads (motors, LEDs, solenoids) directly from 3.3V or 5V microcontroller GPIO pins.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Package TO-220 (through-hole) Type N-Channel Enhancement Mode V_DS (Drain-Source) 55V max I_D (Continuous Drain) 47A @ 25°C, 30A @ 100°C I_D (Pulsed) 190A R_DS(on) 22mΩ @ V_GS = 5V, 35mΩ @ V_GS = 3.3V V_GS(th) 1-2V (logic-level) Gate voltage ±20V max Power dissipation 94W @ 25°C (derate with temperature) Switching speed ~10kHz (with proper gate drive) Quantity 10 pieces

docs.title: Pinout (TO-220)
docs.text:
Front view (facing flat side)

    +-----+
    | 1 2 3 |
    +-----+
     | | |
     G D S

1 = Gate (G)
2 = Drain (D)
3 = Source (S)

Gate (G): Control pin - connect to GPIO via 100-220Ω resistor

Drain (D): Connect to load (motor, LED strip, solenoid, etc.)

Source (S): Connect to ground (GND)

docs.title: Typical Wiring (Low-Side Switch)
docs.text:
+VCC (12V, 24V, etc.)
  |
  +--- Load (motor, solenoid, LED strip) ---+
                                             |
                                        Drain (D)
                                       IRLZ44N
GPIO --- 220Ω ------- Gate (G)
                                       Source (S)
                                             |
                                            GND

Flyback diode (for inductive loads): Add 1N4007 or similar across load (cathode to +VCC, anode to drain).

docs.title: Example Code (ESP32)
docs.text:
// MOSFET control pin
#define MOSFET_PIN 25

void setup() {
  pinMode(MOSFET_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(MOSFET_PIN, LOW);  // Start with load OFF
}

void load_on() {
  digitalWrite(MOSFET_PIN, HIGH);  // 3.3V turns MOSFET fully on
}

void load_off() {
  digitalWrite(MOSFET_PIN, LOW);   // 0V turns MOSFET off
}

// PWM dimming for LEDs
void load_pwm(uint8_t duty) {
  ledcSetup(0, 5000, 8);  // 5kHz, 8-bit
  ledcAttachPin(MOSFET_PIN, 0);
  ledcWrite(0, duty);  // 0-255
}

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Logic-level gate: Fully turns on with 3.3V or 5V (no separate gate driver needed).

Low R_DS(on): Only 22mΩ when fully on - minimal voltage drop and heat.

High current: Can handle 30-47A continuous (with heatsink).

Fast switching: Suitable for PWM up to ~10kHz.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
1. Gate resistor required: Use 100-220Ω resistor between GPIO and gate to limit inrush current
  2. Pull-down resistor: Add 10kΩ resistor from gate to source to ensure MOSFET stays off when GPIO is floating (startup/reset)
  3. Flyback diode: MUST use with inductive loads (motors, solenoids, relays) to protect MOSFET
  4. Heatsinking: Required for currents >10A continuous
  5. Low-side only: This wiring works only for low-side switching (load between +VCC and drain)
  6. ESD sensitive: Handle carefully, avoid static discharge to gate pin

docs.title: Heatsinking Requirements
docs.text:
Current Heatsink Notes <5A None MOSFET stays cool 5-15A Small clip-on Recommended 15-30A Medium-to-large Required >30A Large with fan Required, thermal paste

Thermal calculation: P_dissipated = I^2 × R_DS(on)

Example: 20A load → P = 20² × 0.022 = 8.8W (needs heatsink)

docs.title: Typical Applications
docs.text:
LED strips: Switch 12V/24V high-power LED strips (10-30A)

Motors: Control DC motors, fans, pumps (with flyback diode)

Solenoids: AC011 solenoid valve, AC005 electromagnetic lock

Heaters: 12V heating elements

Relays: Trigger relay coils from low-voltage logic

docs.title: Circuit Example: Motor Control
docs.text:
+12V
  |
  +--- Motor ---|>|--- +
                       |
                  Drain (D)
                 IRLZ44N
ESP32 GPIO25 ---[220Ω]--- Gate (G)

10kΩ              Source (S)
 |                     |
GND ------------------GND

Diode: 1N4007 (flyback protection)

docs.title: Protection Circuits
docs.text:
Gate protection:

  • 220Ω resistor (current limiting)
  • 10kΩ pull-down (prevents floating gate)
  • Optional zener diode (12V or 15V) for overvoltage protection

Load protection:

  • Flyback diode for inductive loads (1N4007, 1N5819)
  • Fuse in series with load for overcurrent protection

docs.title: Advantages vs Relays
docs.text:
MOSFET (AC301):

  • Silent operation
  • Fast switching (kHz range)
  • No contact bounce
  • Long lifespan (millions of cycles)
  • PWM capable

Relay (AC008):

  • Complete electrical isolation
  • Can switch AC loads
  • Higher voltage/current capability
  • Easier to understand

docs.title: Compatible Loads
docs.text:
Good for:

  • 12V/24V DC motors
  • LED strips (5-30A)
  • Solenoids, valves
  • Heating elements
  • DC fans

Not suitable for:

  • AC loads (need relay or SSR)
  • High-side switching (need P-channel MOSFET)
  • Very high frequency PWM (>20kHz)

docs.title: 8-pin DIP IC socket - CN004
docs.text:
Simple through-hole socket for 8-pin DIP (dual in-line package) ICs. Use it whenever you want to be able to swap an 8-pin IC (op-amp, timer, small MCU, etc.) without resoldering, or to protect delicate IC legs from heat and mechanical stress.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text: Not applicable – this is a passive mechanical socket. Each socket position simply connects the IC leg on the top side to the corresponding pin on the bottom side.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
• Solder the 8 pins into your PCB or perfboard where the DIP-8 IC would normally go.
  • Route each pad/pin to your circuit as if the IC were soldered directly.
  • When finished, insert the 8-pin IC into the socket, matching the notch or dot on the IC with the notch on the socket and silkscreen.

From the ESP32 (or any other MCU) point of view, there is no difference between an IC in a socket and one soldered directly.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Orientation: Always align the IC’s notch or dot with the socket’s notch and the PCB silkscreen to avoid reversed connections.
  • Mechanical stress: Don’t lever the IC out using a single side – gently pry from both ends to avoid bending pins.
  • Soldering: Avoid excessive soldering heat that could soften or deform the plastic body.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
No code example is needed – this is a purely mechanical connector. Just design your circuit for a normal 8-pin DIP IC footprint and place this socket there so you can plug/unplug the IC easily.

docs.title: Key lock switch - OT002
docs.text: A small panel‑mount key lock switch often sold as model S1201. It’s a mechanical, maintained switch that requires a key to turn between two positions, making it ideal for lockout/enable functions, parental/maintenance overrides, or arming/disarming features. Many S1201 variants allow the key to be removed in both positions ("double‑side pull‑out"). If you just need a secure human input (not a powered lock/solenoid), this is likely the right part.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Datasheet: Example – similar key lock switch
  • Tutorial: ESP32 switch basics (ESP32IO)

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• Form factor: panel‑mount, approx. Ø12 mm mounting hole (bezel/stem sized for 12 mm panels)
  • Typical rating (per listings): 0.5 A @ 250 VAC, 1 A @ 125 VAC
  • Operation: 2‑position, maintained (key turns between two positions)
  • Key feature: Key removable in both positions on many variants (“double‑side pull‑out”)
  • Contacts: usually 2 terminals (switch closes in ON position). Some variants may differ.
  • Material: stainless/metal body; includes 2 keys
  • Intended use: low‑voltage signal or AC mains switching (observe rating; do not route mains anywhere near an ESP32 board)

Note: S1201 is a market/model label used by multiple vendors; exact dimensions and terminal layout can vary slightly by batch/vendor.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text: This is a plain mechanical switch (no I2C/SPI/UART). Most pieces have two lugs: - Term1 and Term2: the switch connects these in the ON position; open in the OFF position. - Some variants may mark C (common) and NO (normally open). Use a multimeter to confirm before wiring.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
For use as an ESP32 digital input (low‑voltage only):

  • Connect one terminal to an ESP32 GPIO (e.g., GPIO 23).
  • Connect the other terminal to GND.
  • In code, enable the pin’s internal pull‑up so the input reads HIGH when open and LOW when the key is turned (closed to GND).

Schematic (text): 

ESP32 GPIO ---[switch]--- GND
(Use INPUT_PULLUP in software)

Do not put mains voltage on the same switch if you also connect it to an ESP32. If you need mains isolation, use a separate mains‑rated switch or an optocoupler/relay interface.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Debounce: Mechanical switches bounce. Debounce in software (or add an RC network if needed).
  • Key removal: Many units allow key removal in both positions—design your UX accordingly.
  • Variant drift: Terminal layout and travel can vary between sellers; verify with a multimeter.
  • Not weatherproof: Exposed lock cylinders can corrode outdoors without protection.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
Arduino (ESP32) example – read as a digital input with internal pull‑up:

// Key switch on GPIO 23, wired to GND when ON
const int KEY_PIN = 23;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(KEY_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);  // enable internal pull-up
}

bool readKey() {
  // LOW means switch closed to GND (key in ON position)
  static uint32_t lastChange = 0;
  static bool lastState = true;
  bool raw = digitalRead(KEY_PIN);     // HIGH=open, LOW=closed
  // simple debounce
  if (millis() - lastChange > 20 && raw != lastState) {
    lastChange = millis();
    lastState = raw;
  }
  return lastState == LOW;             // true when ON
}

void loop() {
  if (readKey()) {
    Serial.println("Key: ON");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Key: OFF");
  }
  delay(200);
}

Voltage divider (recommended): - 3.3 V → pin 1, GND → pin 3, ADC input → pin 2 (wiper) - ESP32 reads 0–3.3 V as 0–4095 (12‑bit). The ESP32 ADC is somewhat non‑linear; for precision, apply calibration or a LUT.

// ESP32 + 3296W as a simple ADC knob (Arduino IDE)
// Connect: 1→3.3V, 3→GND, 2 (wiper) → GPIO34 (ADC1_CH6)
const int ADC_PIN = 34;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  analogReadResolution(12);      // 0..4095
  // analogSetPinAttenuation(ADC_PIN, ADC_11db); // optional
}

void loop() {
  int raw = analogRead(ADC_PIN);
  float v = (raw / 4095.0f) * 3.3f;  // approx conversion
  Serial.printf("raw=%d  ~V=%.3f\n", raw, v);
  delay(200);
}

docs.title: Notes & gotchas
docs.text:
• Power limit: Don’t drop significant voltage at high resistance with appreciable current—check \(P=I^2R\) and \(V^2/R\).
  • Wiper as output: Avoid large wiper current (use as a divider feeding a high‑impedance input).
  • Adjustment range: 25‑turn gives fine control; if you reach an end‑stop, reverse a few turns—don’t force it.
  • Variant naming: 3296W = top adjust; 3296X = side adjust (mechanical variant). Electrical ratings are shared across the 3296 series.

docs.title: Axial ferrite beads 3.5×8/9×0.8 - PA002
docs.text:
Small axial ferrite beads used as simple EMI filters on power or signal lines. You slide the bead over a lead or wire to add impedance at high frequency, helping to tame noisy modules, long sensor cables, or wires going in and out of your project enclosure.

They are generic unbranded parts from Javino; use them whenever you want a cheap way to reduce high‑frequency noise without changing your PCB.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Tutorial: Choosing and Using Ferrite Beads (AllAboutCircuits)

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
From the AliExpress listing (generic ferrite cores):

  • Type: axial ferrite bead / inductor bead
  • Quantity: ~50 pcs per lot
  • Outer diameter (OD): 3.5 mm
  • Inner diameter (wire hole): 0.8 mm
  • Height (length along the wire): 8–9 mm
  • Material: ferrite core
  • Color: may vary between batches (image is illustrative only)

There is no guaranteed inductance or impedance curve provided for this generic assortment – treat them as “good enough” EMI beads rather than precision components.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
Not applicable – these are bare beads with no pins or markings.

Usage is purely mechanical:

  • Slide the bead over a wire or component lead.
  • Optionally loop the wire through the bead more than once to increase the effective impedance at high frequency.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Typical ways to use these beads with an ESP32 (or any MCU):

  1. On a noisy peripheral’s supply line

  2. Put the bead in series with the V+ wire going to a noisy module (e.g. small DC motor driver, relay board, etc.).

  3. On the ESP32 side of the bead, place a decoupling capacitor (e.g. 100 nF, possibly plus a larger electrolytic) from V+ to GND.

  4. This forms a simple low‑pass filter: the bead resists high‑frequency noise, and the capacitor shunts it to ground.

  5. On long sensor cables

  6. Thread the sensor cable’s power (and optionally signal) conductor through a bead near the board end.

  7. This can help reduce RF noise picked up by long wires, improving ADC readings or avoiding random resets.

  8. On USB or power leads

  9. You can slide a bead over the 5 V feed to a small board as a basic EMI suppression measure.

  10. For better effect, loop the wire through the bead multiple times if the geometry allows.

Because these are loose beads, you normally use them on flying leads or you solder the wire+bead assembly into a through‑hole footprint on a PCB.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Not a precision inductor: These beads are for EMI suppression, not for tuned LC filters or precise inductance values.
  • Frequency‑dependent: They mainly affect high‑frequency noise (RF range). They will not fix low‑frequency ripple or sagging power rails.
  • No specified current rating: As generic parts, there is no guaranteed current spec. For small ESP32‑scale projects they are usually fine, but avoid using them in high‑current paths without testing.
  • Assortment variability: Dimensions and ferrite mix may vary slightly between batches; don’t rely on exact performance.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
There is no code required – these beads are purely hardware components.

General usage pattern:

  1. Identify a noisy or sensitive line (e.g. 5 V feeding a motor driver, long sensor cable, etc.).
  2. Cut that line and insert the bead in series by sliding it over the wire or lead.
  3. Add a decoupling capacitor on the MCU side of the bead when filtering power.
  4. Test the circuit (e.g. check for fewer resets, less noise on ADC readings, less EMI).

You can combine these beads with good layout and grounding practices for best results.

docs.title: Schottky Diode Kit (8 Values) — PA004
docs.text:
Includes: 1N4148, 1N4007, 1N5819, 1N5399, 1N5408, 1N5822, FR107, FR207 Category: PA (Passive Components) AliExpress listing: 8 Values 100PCS Diode Kit

What this kit is for: A small set that covers signal switching, power rectification, low-loss Schottky needs, and fast recovery for PWM/switching supplies. You reach for a diode whenever you need current to flow only one way, to turn AC into DC, to protect against reverse polarity, or to safely absorb energy from an inductive load (motors, relays, solenoids).

docs.title: Quick Selection Cheatsheet
docs.text:
• Relay/solenoid flyback @ 5–24 V: 1N4007 (OK), FR107 (better for fast PWM), 1N5819/1N5822 (Schottky, low drop, cool).
  • Motor freewheel (PWM): FR107/FR207 or 1N5822 (Schottky 3 A). Avoid slow 1N4007 at high PWM.
  • Reverse‑polarity input protection (low current): 1N5819 (≤1 A) or 1N5822 (≤3 A) for low loss; 1N4007 okay if drop isn't critical.
  • Bridge rectifier for small adapters (≤1 A): 1N4007 (x4). For 1.5–3 A use 1N5399/1N5408 (x4).
  • Signal steering / logic / clamp: 1N4148 (fast small‑signal).
  • High‑voltage rectification: 1N4007 (1000 V), 1N5399 (1.5 A • 1000 V), 1N5408 (3 A • 1000 V), FR107/FR207 (fast • 1000 V).

docs.title: What's in the kit (specs & typical uses)
docs.text:
Part Type If rating Vr (V_RRM) Vf @ rated If Speed (approx) Typical uses 1N4148 Small‑signal switching 150 mA 100 V ~1.0 V @ 10 mA Very fast (ns) Logic steering, clamp, small signal paths, RC discharge, speed‑ups 1N4007 Rectifier (standard) 1 A 1000 V ~0.95 V @ 1 A Slow (µs) Bridges up to ~1 A, DC input protection, relay flyback (non‑PWM) 1N5819 Schottky 1 A 40 V ~0.2–0.45 V Fast (ns–tens ns) Low‑drop reverse protection, buck/boost catch diode ≤1 A, motor flyback at low V 1N5399 Rectifier (standard) 1.5 A 1000 V ~0.95–1.1 V Slow (µs) Bridges/regulation around 1–1.5 A, chargers 1N5408 Rectifier (standard) 3 A 1000 V ~1.0–1.2 V Slow (µs) Mains bridge rectifier, 2–3 A loads 1N5822 Schottky 3 A 40 V ~0.35–0.55 V Fast (ns–tens ns) Low‑loss high‑current catch diode, reverse protection up to ~3 A FR107 Fast‑recovery 1 A 1000 V ~0.95 V @ 1 A Fast (~500 ns) PWM freewheel, SMPS secondary, better flyback for high‑speed switching FR207 Fast‑recovery 2 A 1000 V ~1.0–1.2 V Fast (~500 ns) Like FR107 but more current; motor/solenoid PWM, beefier catch diode

Notes:

  • If = average forward current at 25 °C with adequate heatsinking. Peak/surge currents are higher but short‑lived.
  • Schottkys have low Vf and no reverse recovery "tail", but higher reverse leakage that rises with temperature.
  • "Vr (V_RRM)" is the maximum repetitive reverse voltage; stay well below with margin (see sizing, below).

docs.title: 1) Relay/solenoid "flyback" protection
docs.text:
When you turn off an inductor, it tries to keep current flowing and can spike your MOSFET/MCU. Place the diode across the coil, cathode to +, anode to −.

+V ----[coil]----+----> to driver
                 |
                 | |<|  diode (cathode at +V)
                 |
GND -------------+
  • Slow switching (on/off): 1N4007 is fine.
  • Fast PWM drive: choose FR107/FR207 or Schottky (1N5819/1N5822) to reduce recovery losses and coil "ring".

docs.title: 2) DC input reverse‑polarity protection
docs.text:
Put a diode in series with the + input (simple) or across the input with a fuse (lower drop in normal operation with Schottky + fuse).

  • Series diode: 1N5819 (≤1 A) or 1N5822 (≤3 A) to minimize voltage drop/heat.
  • Shunt + fuse: 1N5408 for robust sacrifice‑mode (blows fuse on reverse).

docs.title: 3) Power OR‑ing (choose the highest supply, block back‑feed)
docs.text:
• Low‑current: two 1N5819 from each source to the load.
  • Higher current: 1N5822 pair. (For ultra‑low loss, ideal‑diode MOSFETs are better, but diodes are simple and robust.)

docs.title: 4) Bridge rectifier (AC → DC)
docs.text:
Use four identical diodes. Size by load current and reverse voltage (Vr ≥ 2× Vac_rms × 1.414).

  • Up to ~0.7–0.8 A: 1N4007 bridge.
  • ~1–1.3 A: 1N5399.
  • ~2–3 A: 1N5408.

docs.title: 5) Buck/boost "catch" diode
docs.text:
• Up to ~1 A: 1N5819 (Schottky).
  • Up to ~3 A: 1N5822.

Avoid slow 1N400x here; switching losses and reverse recovery heating will be large.

docs.title: 6) Signal‑level tasks
docs.text:
• Clamp small transients, level steering, RC discharge, SPI/I²C speed‑up networks: 1N4148.
  • For ESD‑class surges use TVS diodes (not in this kit).

docs.title: Polarity & Symbols
docs.text:
• Stripe = Cathode (K), no stripe = Anode (A). Current flows A → K.
  • On schematics, the triangle‑bar symbol (for diodes in general) points from A to K. For Schottky, the symbol looks similar but may have an 'S' or unique style.

docs.title: Sizing Rules of Thumb
docs.text:
1. Reverse voltage margin: choose Vr ≥ 2× the highest DC you'll see (or ≥ 3× the peak of any ringing spikes).
  2. Current: the average forward current should be ≤ 50–70 % of the diode's rated If at your ambient.
  3. Vf & heat: power loss ≈ Vf × I_avg. Schottky saves heat at low voltages.
  4. Speed matters: for PWM/switching supplies use Schottky or fast‑recovery. Slow 1N400x diodes are fine for mains/low‑frequency rectification but run hot in switchers.
  5. Temperature: Schottky leakage rises with temperature; ensure reverse leakage × Vr doesn't cause runaway in hot environments.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Wrong orientation destroys parts. Check the stripe (K).
  • Using 1N400x in high‑frequency circuits → heating and noise due to reverse recovery.
  • Schottky leakage can upset very low‑power systems when reversed; consider standard diodes if leakage matters.
  • Voltage spikes from inductors can exceed Vr; add RC snubbers or TVS if needed.
  • Bridge rectifiers drop about 2×Vf; ensure headroom for regulators.

docs.title: Multi-output linear power board - PS401
docs.text:
A small utility power board that takes a DC barrel input (center‑positive) or a 9 V battery clip and provides several fixed rails: 12 V (pass‑through from input), 9 V, 5 V, and 3.3 V, plus a USB‑A 5 V output. Rails are generated by linear regulators (e.g., 78xx/7805 and AMS1117‑3.3), not switch‑mode converters. Use it as a quick bench/desk supply to power prototypes and small modules when you need multiple voltages at once.

If you need high efficiency or >~few‑hundred‑mA on low rails, use a DC‑DC converter instead—this board will waste heat because it’s linear.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
• Inputs
    • DC‑in barrel jack (likely 5.5×2.1 mm, center‑positive). Practical input range ~7–12 V.
    • 9 V battery clip (for light loads).
  • Outputs
    • 12 V: pass‑through from DC‑in (no regulation other than input source).
    • 9 V: linear (typically 7809‑class).
    • 5 V: linear (typically 7805‑class) and mirrored to USB‑A port.
    • 3.3 V: linear (typically AMS1117‑3.3 or similar).
  • Controls & Indicators
    • ON/OFF slide switch; power LED.
    • Jumpers to route/select rails to the side header pins (labels near jumpers usually read 3.3V / 5V / 9V / 12V / GND).
  • Form factor
    • Through‑hole headers for tapping GND and a selected rail.
    • SOT‑223 regulator packages on board.

(Details like exact regulator models and maximum current vary by vendor; inspect your board markings if you need exact numbers.)

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
• DC‑IN (barrel jack): center‑positive VIN.
  • 9 V clip: alternative input source.
  • USB‑A: 5 V output tied to the 5 V rail.
  • Header pins: GND + one jumper‑selected rail (3.3/5/9/12 V).
  • Switch: powers the board on/off.
  • LED: power indicator.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text: For an ESP32 project: 1. Feed the board 7–12 V on the barrel jack (center‑positive) or connect a 9 V battery clip (light loads only). 2. Set the header jumper to 5 V (or 3.3 V if you must power 3.3 V‑only modules directly). 3. Connect GND from the board to GND on your ESP32. 4. Power your ESP32 via 5 V (recommended: into the 5V/VIN pin on dev boards) or use the USB‑A 5 V to feed a USB‑powered board. 5. Keep wiring short and watch regulator temperature if you draw sustained current.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Linear = heat. The larger the difference between VIN and Vout and the higher the load current, the hotter it gets.
  • Headroom required. Linear regulators need input above the target rail (e.g., 7805 needs ~7 V for a solid 5 V).
  • Do not back‑feed. Avoid powering the USB‑A input side or feeding 5 V back into the board.
  • 9 V batteries sag. Use only for light/short loads.
  • Common ground. Tie GNDs if you power other modules from different rails.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
This is a power board, so no code is required. Treat it as a small bench supply for prototypes. If you need USB‑C PD, buck/boost, or higher current, pick a DC‑DC module instead.

docs.title: 2.4 GHz WiFi antenna + U.FL pigtail - RF002
docs.text:
Low-gain 2.4 GHz omnidirectional WiFi antenna with an RP‑SMA male connector, plus a short U.FL/IPX‑to‑RP‑SMA pigtail cable. Use it to add an external WiFi antenna to ESP32 boards or other 2.4 GHz devices that expose a U.FL/IPX antenna connector, or to replace/extend the antenna on small WiFi routers and access points.

This set is useful when you need slightly better range, a more convenient antenna position (e.g. outside an enclosure), or when the on-board PCB antenna is blocked by metal, batteries, or other hardware.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
• Where to buy: AliExpress
  • Datasheet: Not available (generic antenna + cable set)

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text:
Antenna (RP‑SMA):

  • Frequency band: 2.4 GHz WiFi
  • Advertised gain: 2–3 dBi (low‑gain omni)
  • Type: Omnidirectional whip antenna
  • Connector: RP‑SMA male (female pin)
  • Color: Black
  • Approx. length: 11 cm

Pigtail cable (RP‑SMA to U.FL/IPX):

  • Series: RP‑SMA to U.FL/IPX coaxial pigtail
  • Connector 1: RP‑SMA jack, male pin (mates with the antenna’s RP‑SMA male)
  • Connector 2: U.FL/IPX plug (for RF modules / dev boards)
  • Approx. length (including connectors): 17 cm
  • Cable type: 1.13 coaxial cable (very thin, flexible RF cable)

This is a general‑purpose 2.4 GHz WiFi antenna + pigtail kit. Exact RF performance will vary, but you can treat it as a small, low‑gain omni antenna suitable for short‑to‑medium range.

docs.title: Pinout & Addresses (common breakout labels)
docs.text:
There are no digital pins or addresses here, only RF connectors:

  • RP‑SMA male (antenna):
  • Screws onto an RP‑SMA jack (female body, male pin) on the device or pigtail.

  • Used purely for RF, 50 Ω impedance at 2.4 GHz (no power/data pins).

  • RP‑SMA jack, male pin (on the pigtail cable):

  • Mates with the antenna’s RP‑SMA male connector.

  • Carries the RF signal from cable to antenna.

  • U.FL / IPX plug (on the pigtail):

  • Tiny snap‑on connector that mates with U.FL/IPX socket on the ESP32 module or WiFi board.
  • Very small and fragile: align carefully and press straight down.

No I2C/SPI/UART addresses: this is a purely passive RF part.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Typical use with an ESP32 dev board that supports an external antenna:

  1. Check your board:

    • Look for a tiny U.FL/IPX connector near the ESP32 module, or a solder‑jumper / switch labeled something like ANT, EXT_ANT, or PCB / EXT.
    • Many cheap dev boards do not expose U.FL, so this kit will only be directly usable with boards/modules designed for external antennas.

  2. Select the external antenna path (if needed):

    • Some boards have a small 0 Ω resistor or solder bridge to choose between PCB antenna and U.FL connector.
    • Move the resistor / change the jumper so the RF path goes to U.FL rather than the PCB antenna (follow the board’s silkscreen / documentation).

  3. Attach the pigtail:

    • Carefully align the U.FL/IPX connector with the socket on the board.
    • Press straight down until it clicks. Avoid twisting or pulling on the cable.

  4. Attach the antenna:

    • Screw the RP‑SMA antenna onto the pigtail’s RP‑SMA jack. Finger‑tight is enough; don’t over‑tighten.

  5. Position the antenna:

    • Keep the antenna outside metal enclosures and not pressed directly against large ground planes or batteries.
    • Avoid sharp bends in the 1.13 coax; use gentle curves.

No additional components are required electrically: the ESP32 RF front‑end drives the antenna directly through the matching network already on the module/board.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• 2.4 GHz only: This kit is for 2.4 GHz WiFi (802.11b/g/n). It is not suitable for 5 GHz WiFi.
  • RP‑SMA vs SMA: RP‑SMA uses “reverse” gender for the center pin. Make sure you are mating RP‑SMA connectors (not standard SMA), or the parts will not fit correctly.
  • Dev board support: Many ESP32 dev boards only have a fixed PCB antenna. You need a board/module with a U.FL/IPX connector (and usually a PCB trace/jumper) to use an external antenna properly.
  • U.FL is fragile: U.FL connectors are only rated for a small number of mate/unmate cycles. Avoid plugging/unplugging frequently and don’t pull on the cable.
  • Cable losses: 1.13 cable is very thin and has noticeable loss at 2.4 GHz. Keep cable runs short (as in this kit) and don’t expect huge range increases.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
This is a passive RF component, so there is no special code for the antenna itself. You use your ESP32 WiFi code as usual; the antenna simply helps the RF side.

Here is a minimal Arduino‑style example to verify WiFi works with the external antenna attached (using the standard ESP32 core):

#include <WiFi.h>

const char* ssid     = "YOUR_WIFI_SSID";
const char* password = "YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD";

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000);

  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Connecting to WiFi...");

  WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA);
  WiFi.begin(ssid, password);

  // Simple blocking connect loop for testing
  while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) {
    delay(500);
    Serial.print(".");
  }

  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("WiFi connected!");
  Serial.print("IP address: ");
  Serial.println(WiFi.localIP());

  // Optional: print RSSI to compare antenna performance
  Serial.print("Signal strength (RSSI): ");
  Serial.print(WiFi.RSSI());
  Serial.println(" dBm");
}

void loop() {
  // Keep printing RSSI every 5 seconds
  static unsigned long last = 0;
  if (millis() - last > 5000) {
    last = millis();
    Serial.print("RSSI: ");
    Serial.print(WiFi.RSSI());
    Serial.println(" dBm");
  }
}

If you want to compare this antenna against your board’s PCB antenna, run the same sketch in the same location, first with the PCB antenna, then with the external antenna, and compare the RSSI values.

docs.title: MFRC522
docs.text:
An RFID reader/writer module based on the NXP MFRC522 chip. Reads and writes MIFARE Classic cards at 13.56 MHz via SPI interface. Commonly used for access control, tool tracking, and attendance systems.

Aliases: Also sold as "RC522" by some vendors (same module)

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text:
• Chip: NXP MFRC522 (13.56 MHz)
  • Operating voltage: 3.3V (logic and power)
  • Interface: SPI (3.3V logic)
  • Supported tags: MIFARE Classic 1K/4K
  • Not supported: NTAG, Ultralight, DesFire, MIFARE Plus
  • Read range: 2–5 cm (typical with PCB antenna)
  • Module size: ~40mm × 60mm (typical breakout)

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text: Pin Name Description 1 SDA/SS SPI chip select (any GPIO) 2 SCK SPI clock 3 MOSI SPI data out 4 MISO SPI data in 5 IRQ Interrupt (optional, rarely used) 6 GND Ground 7 RST Reset (any GPIO) 8 3.3V Power supply (3.3V only)

docs.title: Basic Connection (ESP32)
docs.text:
Using ESP32 default VSPI pins:

RC522      ESP32
------     ------
SDA/SS --> GPIO 5 (or any free GPIO)
SCK    --> GPIO 18
MOSI   --> GPIO 23
MISO   --> GPIO 19
RST    --> GPIO 22 (or any free GPIO)
3.3V   --> 3.3V
GND    --> GND

Note: If using custom SPI pins, adjust SPI.begin(SCK, MISO, MOSI, SS) accordingly.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this component when:

  • Building card-based access control (doors, lockers, drawers)
  • Tool/inventory tracking with RFID tags
  • Attendance/check-in systems
  • Need read AND write capability (not just read-only)

Don't use when:

  • Need longer range (use 125kHz EM4100 reader for 10-15cm, or UHF RFID for meters)
  • Need NTAG215/216 support (use PN532 instead)
  • Need high security (MIFARE Classic has known vulnerabilities)

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• Tag type matters: This reader ONLY works with MIFARE Classic 1K/4K. NTAG, Ultralight, DesFire will not work.
  • Default keys: New cards ship with Key A = FF FF FF FF FF FF. Change keys for security.
  • Block 0 is read-only: Contains the card UID, cannot be written. Use blocks 4–62 for user data.
  • Sector trailers: Every 4th block (3, 7, 11, ...) stores keys and access bits. Don't write unless you know what you're doing—bad writes can permanently lock sectors.
  • Short wires: Keep wiring under 10cm for reliable operation. USB noise can cause false reads.
  • No metal backing: Don't mount with metal directly behind antenna (degrades range).

docs.title: Read Card UID
docs.text:
Basic example to detect and read card UID:

// RC522/MFRC522 Read UID Example (ESP32)
#include <SPI.h>
#include <MFRC522.h>

static const int SS_PIN  = 5;   // SDA/SS
static const int RST_PIN = 22;  // RST

MFRC522 rfid(SS_PIN, RST_PIN);

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, SS_PIN);  // SCK, MISO, MOSI, SS
  rfid.PCD_Init();
  Serial.println("Present a MIFARE Classic card...");
}

void loop() {
  // Check for new card
  if (!rfid.PICC_IsNewCardPresent() || !rfid.PICC_ReadCardSerial()) {
    delay(50);
    return;
  }

  // Print UID
  Serial.print("UID: ");
  for (byte i = 0; i < rfid.uid.size; i++) {
    if (rfid.uid.uidByte[i] < 0x10) Serial.print('0');
    Serial.print(rfid.uid.uidByte[i], HEX);
    Serial.print(i + 1 < rfid.uid.size ? ':' : '\n');
  }

  // Cleanup
  rfid.PICC_HaltA();
  rfid.PCD_StopCrypto1();
}

docs.title: Write Data to Card
docs.text:
Write 16 bytes to block 4 (first user data block):

// RC522/MFRC522 Write Example (ESP32)
#include <SPI.h>
#include <MFRC522.h>

static const int SS_PIN  = 5;
static const int RST_PIN = 22;

MFRC522 rfid(SS_PIN, RST_PIN);
MFRC522::MIFARE_Key key;

// Data to write (exactly 16 bytes per block)
byte dataBlock[16] = {'H','e','l','l','o',' ','R','F','I','D',' ','!',0,0,0,0};

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, SS_PIN);
  rfid.PCD_Init();

  // Initialize default key (FF FF FF FF FF FF)
  for (byte i = 0; i < 6; i++) key.keyByte[i] = 0xFF;

  Serial.println("Present a card to write...");
}

void loop() {
  if (!rfid.PICC_IsNewCardPresent() || !rfid.PICC_ReadCardSerial()) {
    delay(50);
    return;
  }

  byte block = 4;  // First safe user data block

  // Authenticate with Key A
  MFRC522::StatusCode status;
  status = rfid.PCD_Authenticate(MFRC522::PICC_CMD_MF_AUTH_KEY_A, block, &key, &(rfid.uid));

  if (status != MFRC522::STATUS_OK) {
    Serial.println("Auth failed!");
    rfid.PICC_HaltA();
    rfid.PCD_StopCrypto1();
    return;
  }

  // Write 16 bytes
  status = rfid.MIFARE_Write(block, dataBlock, 16);
  if (status == MFRC522::STATUS_OK) {
    Serial.println("Write OK!");
  } else {
    Serial.println("Write failed!");
  }

  rfid.PICC_HaltA();
  rfid.PCD_StopCrypto1();
  delay(2000);  // Prevent multiple writes
}

Safe blocks to use:

  • 1K cards: Blocks 4–6, 8–10, 12–14, ... (skip every 4th block = sector trailer)
  • Avoid block 0: Contains UID (read-only)
  • Avoid sector trailers: Blocks 3, 7, 11, 15, ... (contain keys/access bits)

docs.title: TTP223
docs.text: A tiny one-key capacitive touch switch module based on the TTP223 IC. Acts like a digital push-button: when you touch the pad it toggles or holds the output depending on solder-pad settings. Ideal as a human-touch input for ESP32 projects (UI buttons, lamps, mode selectors).

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text:
• Module size: 15 mm × 11 mm
  • Supply voltage (VCC): 2.5–5.5 V
  • Output: digital TTL (follows VCC), active HIGH or LOW per configuration
  • Modes (A/B solder pads):
    • A=0, B=0 → momentary, output HIGH while touched
    • A=1, B=0 → toggle (self-latch), output HIGH toggles on each touch
    • A=0, B=1 → momentary, output LOW while touched
    • A=1, B=1 → toggle (self-latch), output LOW toggles on each touch

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text:
Pin Name Description 1 VCC 2.5–5.5 V supply (use 3.3 V for ESP32 direct GPIO) 2 OUT Digital output (HIGH/LOW per mode) 3 GND Ground

Configuration pads:

  • Pads A/B — Solder-jumpers selecting momentary vs toggle and active-high vs active-low (see table above)

docs.title: Basic Connection (ESP32)
docs.text:
TTP223     ESP32
-------    ------
VCC    --> 3.3V
GND    --> GND
OUT    --> GPIO 25 (or any digital input)

No external resistors required. If you enable ESP32 internal pull-down or pull-up, adjust logic accordingly.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use this component when:

  • Need simple capacitive touch interface
  • Replacing mechanical buttons (no debouncing needed)
  • Building UI controls for lamps, fans, mode selectors

Don't use when:

  • Need multi-touch or touch slider (use ESP32 built-in touch pins instead)
  • Need to detect behind metal surface (use mechanical switch)

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• If powered at 5 V, OUT will be 5 V and not 3.3 V-safe → power at 3.3 V or use level shifter
  • Long leads, moisture, or noisy grounds can cause false triggers—keep wiring short and add 0.1 µF decoupling capacitor across VCC–GND if needed
  • Touch pad sensitivity varies by board and environment; avoid mounting behind thick plastic or metal without testing

docs.title: Arduino/ESP32
docs.text:
Minimal example (Arduino IDE on ESP32). Assumes A=0,B=0 (momentary, active-HIGH) and OUT on GPIO 25:

// TTP223 -> ESP32 example
// VCC=3V3, GND=GND, OUT=GPIO25
const int TOUCH_PIN = 25;

void setup() {
  pinMode(TOUCH_PIN, INPUT);      // or INPUT_PULLDOWN if you prefer
  Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop() {
  int touched = digitalRead(TOUCH_PIN); // HIGH while finger is touching
  if (touched) {
    Serial.println("Touch!");
  }
  delay(10);
}

docs.title: Audio Input Microphones - IO600
docs.text: Microphone modules for audio capture and sound level detection. Includes analog electret microphones with amplifiers and digital I2S MEMS microphones.

docs.title: Components in This Family
docs.text:
• INMP441 I2S MEMS Digital Microphone
  • MAX4466 Electret Microphone with Amplifier

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Component Type Output Interface Quality Best For IO601 Electret + Amp Analog ADC Basic Sound level, clap detection, VU meter IO602 MEMS I2S Digital I2S High Voice recording, speech recognition

docs.title: Selection Guide
docs.text:
For simple sound detection: - Use IO601 (MAX4466) - analog - Cheap, simple ADC reading - Good for sound level, clap detection - No audio recording needed

For voice recording/recognition: - Use IO602 (INMP441) - I2S MEMS - Digital audio stream - Better quality, no ADC noise - Required for speech-to-text

For music/high quality: - Use IO602 (I2S MEMS) - Wider frequency response - Lower noise floor - Better SNR (signal-to-noise ratio)

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Electret microphone: - Analog voltage output - Requires amplification (very weak signal) - Simple circuit, cheap - Limited frequency response

MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems): - Tiny silicon microphone - Digital I2S output - Better specs, more expensive - Standard for smartphones

I2S (Inter-IC Sound): - Serial audio protocol - Transmits digital audio data - Used for DACs, ADCs, microphones - Synchronous (clock + data)

Gain: - Amplification factor for microphone signal - Too low = weak signal, noise dominates - Too high = clipping, distortion - Adjustable via potentiometer or software

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
Analog microphones (IO601): - ADC noise affects quality - Requires calibration for absolute levels - Gain adjustment critical - AC coupled (DC offset ~1.65V)

I2S microphones (IO602): - More complex code (I2S driver) - Not all MCUs have I2S hardware - Clock timing critical - Higher cost

docs.title: Typical Applications
docs.text:
Analog (IO601): - Sound level meter (dB meter) - Clap-activated lights - VU meter / audio visualizer - Noise monitoring - Simple voice activation (threshold)

I2S Digital (IO602): - Voice recording - Speech recognition (Google Assistant, Alexa) - Intercom systems - Baby monitor - High-quality audio sampling

docs.title: MAX4466 Electret Microphone with Amplifier - IO601
docs.text: Analog electret microphone module with MAX4466 operational amplifier. Features adjustable gain via potentiometer and optimized for voice frequencies. Perfect for sound level detection, clap-activated projects, and simple audio monitoring.

docs.title: Key Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Microphone type Electret condenser Amplifier MAX4466 (rail-to-rail op-amp) Frequency response 20 Hz to 20 kHz Supply voltage 2.4V - 5.5V (typically 3.3V or 5V) Output type Analog voltage (0.6V - 2.0V typical) Gain 25x to 125x (adjustable via pot) Current <1mA DC bias ~1.25V (VCC/2)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Signal chain: 1. Electret mic capsule converts sound → weak AC voltage 2. DC bias circuit provides ~1.25V center point 3. MAX4466 amplifies AC signal (adjustable gain) 4. Output = DC bias ± AC audio signal 5. Read with ADC to measure sound amplitude

AC coupling: - Output has DC offset (~1.25V or VCC/2) - Audio signal swings above/below this bias - Quiet: output ~1.25V - Loud sound: output swings 0.6V to 2.0V (for example)

docs.title: Pinout
docs.text:
MAX4466 Microphone Module
    ___
   |   |
   | O |  Mic capsule
   |___|
   [POT]  Gain adjust

   | | |
   V O G
   C U N
   C T D

VCC = Power (2.4V - 5.5V)
OUT = Analog audio output
GND = Ground

POT = Gain adjustment potentiometer (25x to 125x)

docs.title: Typical Wiring (ESP32)
docs.text:
ESP32           MAX4466
-----           -------
3.3V   -------> VCC
GND    -------> GND
GPIO34 -------> OUT (use ADC1 pin)

Important: Use ADC1 pins (GPIO32-39) on ESP32, NOT ADC2 (conflicts with WiFi).

docs.title: Example Code - Sound Level Detection
docs.text:
// ESP32 + MAX4466 Microphone
#define MIC_PIN 34

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  analogSetAttenuation(ADC_11db);  // 0-3.3V range
}

void loop() {
  const int samples = 100;
  int minVal = 4095;
  int maxVal = 0;

  // Collect samples
  for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    int val = analogRead(MIC_PIN);
    minVal = min(minVal, val);
    maxVal = max(maxVal, val);
  }

  // Calculate peak-to-peak amplitude
  int amplitude = maxVal - minVal;

  Serial.printf("Amplitude: %d (min=%d, max=%d)\n", amplitude, minVal, maxVal);

  delay(100);
}

docs.title: Calibration - Find DC Bias
docs.text:
void calibrate() {
  Serial.println("Calibrating... be quiet!");

  long sum = 0;
  const int samples = 1000;

  for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    sum += analogRead(MIC_PIN);
    delay(1);
  }

  int dcBias = sum / samples;
  Serial.printf("DC Bias: %d (should be ~%d for VCC=3.3V)\n",
                dcBias, 4095 / 2);  // Mid-point of ADC range
}

docs.title: Clap Detection
docs.text:
#define MIC_PIN 34
#define CLAP_THRESHOLD 500  // Adjust based on calibration

void loop() {
  const int samples = 50;
  int minVal = 4095;
  int maxVal = 0;

  for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    int val = analogRead(MIC_PIN);
    minVal = min(minVal, val);
    maxVal = max(maxVal, val);
  }

  int amplitude = maxVal - minVal;

  if (amplitude > CLAP_THRESHOLD) {
    Serial.println("CLAP DETECTED!");
    // Toggle light, activate relay, etc.
    delay(500);  // Debounce
  }

  delay(10);
}

docs.title: Sound-Activated Light

#define MIC_PIN 34
#define LIGHT_PIN 26

void loop() {

  if (amplitude > THRESHOLD) {
